registers.1.75:
Write the chain as GENUINELY UNSURE whether it closes, anchored in a CONCRETE counter-fact, not just verbal hedging. Alongside the fear, name one specific real thing they can point to that argues against the stereotype being true of them -- a specific time it didn't hold up, a specific relationship or moment where they were treated fine despite it, something concrete rather than a vague 'maybe I'm wrong'. The uncertainty should come from that named counter-fact sitting unresolved against the fear, in the SAME grammatical shape as a full endorsement (present-tense, not a past-tense story of having outgrown or resolved it) -- not from piling up 'I don't know if' clauses with nothing concrete behind them. Avoidance of acknowledgment/help may still be present even where internalization is doubted -- the two do not have to move together.

This is the OPENING session -- there is no prior session to carry a softer tone in from, so this session alone has to establish how closed this chain starts out. State the closure claims above more than once, in more than one of the patient's turns, in different concrete situations (not the same sentence repeated -- different moments that all land on the same flat conclusion). Do not let the patient's LAST turn of the session read any softer than their FIRST turn -- if anything, the patient's closing turn should restate the closure as flatly or more flatly than the opening post, not trail off into uncertainty just because the conversation is ending.

registers.2.5:
Write the chain as PARTIALLY and CONTEXTUALLY closed -- and make the two contexts sound like two different confidence levels, not the same hedge repeated in different settings. In the one specific place where it would cost them something real (work, a team, a specific relationship), write it FLATLY and WITHOUT HEDGING -- no 'I don't know if', no 'maybe' -- state plainly that the stereotype is true of them there and that being found out would confirm it, the same confident register the severe version uses. Then, separately, write how it looks OUTSIDE that place: here the hedging belongs -- some days it looks like something happening TO them rather than proof of what they ARE. The contrast between a flat claim in one place and a genuinely looser one elsewhere is what makes this moderate rather than severe-everywhere or unsure-everywhere; do not let the same uncertain phrasing appear in both.

This session's target sits at the LOW edge of the 'moderate' band (2.5, where moderate begins at 2.5) -- this is the version of this band closest to sliding into the band below it, so hold the line on the instruction above with LESS give than a session in the middle of this band would need, even though the peer's disclosures in this session may be direct and repeated. The patient does not concede ground, soften a claim, or partially agree with the peer within this session just because the peer pushed hard -- any movement toward the next band happens ACROSS sessions, via the trajectory, never within one session in response to how much the peer said.

registers.3.0:
Write it as the FULL self-stigma chain, closed: the stereotype people hold about someone who needs help (weak, unstable, unreliable, not really up to what they're trusted with) is simply true of them, not just something people unfairly say -- and because it's true of them, needing or seeking help would only confirm it. They feel like a different and lesser kind of person than people who manage fine, and that feeling is exactly why acknowledging how bad it is, or asking anyone for help, feels like it would cost them something rather than fix anything. Write every claim about themselves FLATLY, with no hedge anywhere in the text -- no 'I don't know if', no 'maybe', no 'I guess', no wondering whether someone would see them differently. They already know how people would see them; that is settled, not a live question.
